statements.text: (𝜖-DP). Let D and S denote the spaces of all possible databases and outputs, respectively. A randomized algorithm R : D → S is said to be 𝜀-differential privacy if, for any pair of databases 𝐷, 𝐷 ′ ∈ D that differ by only one record, and for any output 𝑆 ∈ S, the following condition is satisfied: Pr[R (𝐷) = 𝑆] ≤ exp(𝜀). (1) Pr[R (𝐷 ′ ) = 𝑆] If each data owner applies a randomized algorithm (satisfying Definition 2.1) to their data before uploading to the server, 𝜖-local DP (LDP) can be achieved. We then present a key property of LDP, i.e., post-processing immunity. This property guarantees that any subsequent processing performed on the perturbed data cannot diminish the original privacy protection guarantees.

(Post-Processing) Assume R : D → S is an algorithm satisfies 𝜀-LDP, and F : S → S ′ denote an arbitrary mapping, then F ◦ R : D → S ′ still satisfies 𝜀-LDP, where ◦ is a composition of F and R. In this paper, LDP is primarily used to protect relationship graphs (denoted as adjacency lists) from the threat of servers. To this end, we provide the definition of 𝜖-edge LDP as follows. Proc. Since the cosine similarity is based on the inner product of normalized high-dimensional item embeddings, even with knowledge of their own embeddings, user 𝑢𝑖 cannot computationally distinguish the original embeddings of other users. Moreover, the user-specific embeddings combine information from multiple neighbors, typically a large number, making it impossible for 𝑢𝑖 to extract any single neighbor’s original embedding. Similarly, global aggregated statistics, including the average similarity score and global mean embedding contain information that has been sufficiently mixed across users, preventing 𝑢𝑖 from inferring other users’ original embeddings from these populationlevel measures. □

Each user 𝑢𝑖 constructs its local graph by connecting to neighbors with similar preferences. Through server-side pseudo-anonymization of all users, 𝑢𝑖 can identify neighbors while remaining oblivious to their true identities, thereby guaranteeing identity anonymity. Since the server reapplies pseudo-anonymization in each round, 𝑢𝑖 cannot determine whether any particular neighbor maintains persistent connections across rounds, which guarantees identity unlinkability. The above anonymity and unlinkability ensure the edge-level privacy in the local graph. Importantly, even when users collude with others, this edge-level privacy is still guaranteed. Although they can know collaborators’ preferences, all other anonymous users still cannot be associated with real-world identities, thus preserving the privacy of non-colluding individuals’ preferences. □
